---
title: "2.3 Linear Interaction Effects"
---

> *"Interaction effects exist when the effect of one independent variable is contingent on the level of another independent variable. For example, does the effect of obtaining more education depend on whether someone is white or black? Does the effect of aging depend on whether someone is a man or a woman?"* ([Mize 2019 p.81](https://www.sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/))

- Interaction effects are also known as moderation (i.e., one IV moderates the effect of another IV)
- Can allow the effect of one IV to vary across levels of another IV by including a product term of the two variables in the model
  - Multiply the two IVs together
  - Include the two original IVs *and* the product term in the model

## Interaction effect example and interpretation

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(modelsummary)    # regression tables
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta")

# Keep only model vars and drop any missing data on them
gss <- gss[c("occprest", "age", "woman", "college")]
gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss), ]

# Treat binary variables as factors using their value labels
gss <- gss |> mutate(woman = as_factor(woman), college = as_factor(college))

intmod <- lm(occprest ~ age * woman + college, data = gss)

modelsummary(intmod, stars = c("*" = .05, "**" = .01, "***" = .001),
  title = "[2.3.a] Occupational prestige linear regression model: Interaction between age & gender")
```

:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
For linear additive effects, the coefficient on the product term tests whether there is an interactive relationship between the two IVs (i.e., whether the effect of one variable *depends on* the level of another variable). **This is only the case for linear additive effects**

> *The effect of age on occupational prestige is different for men and women (interaction term p \< 0.001)*

What is the effect of age for men? For women? Because "woman" is coded as 1, *β~age~* tells us the effect of age for men (when *woman* = 0). The effect of age for women = *β~age~* + *β~woman\ X\ age~* which is 0.072 -- 0.055 = 0.017. **Again, this is only the case for linear additive effects.** I generally go straight to plotting predictions with interactions
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. qui margins, at(age=(20(5)80) woman=(0 1))

. marginsplot, ///
>     title("[2.3.b] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age and G
> ender", size(medium)) ///
>     subtitle("Interaction Term: Gender X Age") ///
>     ytitle("Occupational Prestige") ///
>     recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs14)) ylab(38(2)46)

Variables that uniquely identify margins: age woman

```

![](fig/cda-02_03_b-interaction-1.png){width=80% fig-alt="Predicted occupational prestige by age for men and women: two straight lines that cross, with a steeper slope for men."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Predicted occupational prestige by age for men and women: two straight lines that cross, with a steeper slope for men."
plot_predictions(intmod, by = c("age", "woman"),
  newdata = datagrid(age = seq(20, 80, 5), woman = unique,
    grid_type = "counterfactual")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(38, 46, 2), limits = c(38, 46)) +
  labs(title = "[2.3.b] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age and Gender",
    subtitle = "Interaction Term: Gender X Age",
    x = "Age", y = "Occupational Prestige")
```

:::

### Marginal effects by levels of another variable

- With linear effects, we can calculate the slope for each level of the nominal variable (here, *woman*) by adding the coefficients
  - But, the coefficients don't provide a significance test for the effect of *age* for woman=1
- Marginal effects straightforwardly provide this, without the need for mental math

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. est restore opintmod
(results opintmod are active now)

. mecompare age, by(woman)

Predicting: Linear prediction
Marginal effects (N_m1=58304)

                                 |  ME #   Estimate         SE      P>|z|
---------------------------------+---------------------------------------
age + 1 (centered)               |                                       
                             Men |     1      0.072      0.004      0.000
                           Women |     2      0.017      0.004      0.000

```

## R

```{r}
avg_comparisons(intmod, variables = list(age = 1), by = "woman")
```

:::

- Easy to test the equality of the marginal effects; in the case of linear effects, will provide equivalent answer to interaction coefficients (but only in this case!)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. metest 2 - 1

                                 |  estimate         se     pvalue 
---------------------------------+--------------------------------
       age_woman_1 - age_woman_0 |    -0.055      0.006      0.000 

```

## R

```{r}
avg_comparisons(intmod, variables = list(age = 1), by = "woman",
  hypothesis = ~ pairwise)
```

:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
**R**: Use **hypothesis** option of **avg_comparisons**
:::
